title: Why Are People Having Fewer Babies? The Data Explained

segments.label: scene 1 (title)
segments.text: Something quiet but monumental is reshaping our world. Across recent decades, fewer people are choosing to have children, driving a dramatic fall in fertility.

segments.label: scene 2 (counter)
segments.text: Back in 1960, the US fertility rate reached a high of 3.65 births per woman. Large families were a cornerstone of American life.

segments.label: scene 3 (line)
segments.text: That picture changed rapidly over the following decades. By 1970, the rate fell to 2.48, and hit 1.77 by 1975.

segments.label: scene 4 (compare)
segments.text: Between 1960 and 2024, America's birth rate plunged by 55%. That represents a fundamental transformation in societal structure.

segments.label: scene 5 (counter)
segments.text: Even after brief rebounds, like reaching 2.08 in 1990, rates continued sliding downward through 2020.

segments.label: scene 6 (line)
segments.text: In 2023, the rate touched an all-time low of 1.62, before ticking up slightly to 1.63 in 2024.

segments.label: scene 7 (statement)
segments.text: This historic drop isn't just a statistical blip. It marks a deep structural shift that will reverberate for generations.

segments.label: scene 8 (statement)
segments.text: To truly understand today's birth rate decline, we have to rewind to the post-war era. The mid-twentieth century was defined by a massive demographic surge.

segments.label: scene 9 (line)
segments.text: According to the World Bank, American fertility reached its absolute peak right at the opening of the decade in 1960. Families were larger than they had been in generations.

segments.label: scene 10 (counter)
segments.text: That dramatic climb did not last forever. By 1965, the fertility rate fell swiftly to 2.91 births per woman.

segments.label: scene 11 (compare)
segments.text: Measuring from that 1965 milestone down to 2024, American birth rates have plummeted by 44%.

segments.label: scene 12 (statement)
segments.text: This initial drop was driven by profound social progress. Expanding educational opportunities and widespread family planning gave people new control over their lives.

segments.label: scene 13 (compare)
segments.text: By 1970, the slide was well underway, with rates sitting 34% above current levels before dropping further.

segments.label: scene 14 (gauge)
segments.text: What began as a return to normal after a baby boom soon established a brand new baseline for family size.

segments.label: scene 15 (counter)
segments.text: After the steep drops of earlier decades, the decline temporarily paused. By January 1980, American fertility stabilized at 1.84 births per woman.

segments.label: scene 16 (statement)
segments.text: Changing economic realities and dual-income households established a brand new baseline for family sizes across the country.

segments.label: scene 17 (line)
segments.text: A modest mini-boom followed heading into the new millennium. By January 2000, the fertility rate climbed back up to 2.06.

segments.label: scene 18 (counter)
segments.text: That momentum proved remarkably steady for several years. By January 2005, the rate held firm at 2.06, remaining 21% above current levels.

segments.label: scene 19 (counter)
segments.text: However, broader economic pressures soon ended that plateau. By January 2010, fertility dropped to 1.93, representing a 16% drop compared to 2024.

segments.label: scene 20 (line)
segments.text: The downward slope gathered pace throughout the following decade. By January 2015, the rate fell back down to 1.84 births per woman.

segments.label: scene 21 (counter)
segments.text: Just before global disruptions hit, birth rates sank even lower. By January 2020, fertility settled at 1.64, setting up historic lows.

segments.label: scene 22 (statement)
segments.text: Following the fallout of the Great Recession, economic shocks permanently altered how young adults approached building a family.

segments.label: scene 23 (statement)
segments.text: Surging housing prices paired with escalating student debt forced many young couples to continually postpone major traditional milestones.

segments.label: scene 24 (compare)
segments.text: Securing financial stability and advancing personal careers became essential prerequisites long before most couples even contemplated parenthood.

segments.label: scene 25 (line)
segments.text: Looking from January 2015 to January 2024, fertility dropped another 12%, showing how temporary delays turned into permanent choices.

segments.label: scene 26 (statement)
segments.text: Simultaneously, evolving cultural expectations encouraged more women to pursue higher education, professional autonomy, and independent life goals.

segments.label: scene 27 (line)
segments.text: Between January 2020 and January 2024, birth rates slipped an additional 1%, reflecting lingering economic uncertainty and pandemic disruptions.

segments.label: scene 28 (line)
segments.text: Though rates saw a slight 0.6% gain in the final year, America's low fertility era remains deeply entrenched.

segments.label: scene 29 (compare)
segments.text: Minor annual upticks can easily mask a long-term demographic reality.

segments.label: scene 30 (statement)
segments.text: Across recent decades, lower fertility has fundamentally reshaped standard household structures. Smaller families mean fewer siblings, fewer cousins, and steadily shrinking extended networks.

segments.label: scene 31 (line)
segments.text: When birth rates sit below demographic replacement levels, overall population growth stalls. Over time, society gradually transitions toward a much older population structure.

segments.label: scene 32 (statement)
segments.text: A shrinking ratio of active workers to retirees places unprecedented strain on social safety nets. Maintaining public pensions and healthcare systems becomes increasingly difficult.

segments.label: scene 33 (gauge)
segments.text: Local communities must also adapt as youth populations contract. Public investment naturally shifts away from schools and child services toward elder care.

segments.label: scene 34 (statement)
segments.text: Long-term economic dynamism can also cool as workforce expansion slows. Fewer young adults enter the market, dampening consumer demand and overall innovation.

segments.label: scene 35 (gauge)
segments.text: Small annual fluctuations do not change this overarching trajectory. Compact household structures are now firmly established as the modern default.

segments.label: scene 36 (statement)
segments.text: America's demographic shift is not a sudden collapse, but a quiet, decades-long restructuring of modern family life across the nation.

segments.label: scene 37 (statement)
segments.text: Broader access to higher education, evolving career ambitions, and persistent housing costs have fundamentally reshaped household decisions.

segments.label: scene 38 (compare)
segments.text: Compared to January 1975, the national birth rate has dropped another 8%, establishing compact families as the modern norm.

segments.label: scene 39 (gauge)
segments.text: Current fertility levels sit near historic lows, reflecting structural economic patterns that minor policy adjustments cannot quickly reverse.

segments.label: scene 40 (line)
segments.text: Measured against January 1995, fertility has declined 18%, illustrating how temporary delays in milestones gradually became permanent choices.

segments.label: scene 41 (statement)
segments.text: Ultimately, modern demographic contraction reflects deeply entrenched socioeconomic realities rather than fleeting cultural shifts.
